title: Wildlife Utilization and Trade in Urban Markets of the West Region of Cameroon: Patterns, Socioeconomic Drivers and Conservation Implications
content:
ABSTRACT

The wild meat trade remains a significant ecological and socio-economic issue across sub-Saharan Africa. In Cameroon's West Region, urban markets play a central role in the commercialization of wild animal products; however, information on the species composition, utilization patterns, market-level variation and economic characteristics of this trade remains limited. This study investigated the diversity, utilization patterns, spatial variation and economic value of wild terrestrial vertebrate species sold in 16 markets across the region. A total of 476 wild animal specimens were recorded, representing 46 species from 33 families, 18 orders and three vertebrate classes (Mammalia, Reptilia, Aves). Meat was the most frequently recorded body part and was primarily associated with food use, whereas skins, feathers and snake oil were recorded mainly for cultural and medicinal purposes. Most records involved species that were classified as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List, although Near Threatened, Vulnerable, endangered and Critically Endangered species were also recorded, including yellow-backed duiker (Cephalophus silvicultur), African leopard (Panthera pardus) and gorilla (Gorilla gorilla). Generalized linear models indicated an association between market price and IUCN category, national wildlife protection level, purpose of utilization and taxonomic class. Near Threatened and Class A species had higher observed prices in the study dataset. Threatened and protected species were particularly represented in the Bangangte and Santchou markets. These findings identify market-level patterns that can inform wildlife monitoring and enforcement while highlighting the need to consider species availability, market access and other unmeasured factors when interpreting price differences. Because this study did not measure population abundance, hunting effort, consumer demand, or disease transmission, the findings should be interpreted as associations observed within the surveyed markets rather than estimates of population-level impacts or causal effects.
